analysis.title: The risks reshaping global AI investment (UBS House View - Daily US)
key_insights: NVIDIA shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday, pulling Nasdaq futures about 1% lower and pressuring tech-heavy markets in Taiwan and South Korea. The move followed reports that NVIDIA's board met Wednesday night to discuss whether CEO Jensen Huang should remain in his role, after news that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

UBS says investors are becoming more selective on the AI trade. Recent tech volatility reflects a shift from rewarding spending commitments toward assessing monetization, balance sheet strength, capacity utilization and prospective returns.

Underlying AI demand remains robust: recent earnings showed accelerating cloud revenue and expanding orders for computing capacity. UBS forecasts aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026 and USD 1.4tr in 2027.

Key-person risk warrants greater attention. Leadership and governance can become material investment considerations when a company's strategy and standing are closely tied to one individual, particularly after AI equity gains concentrated in a narrow group of businesses. Succession planning may matter alongside earnings growth.

UBS believes recent developments reduce the likelihood of an easing in current restrictions on advanced AI-chip shipments to China, and scrutiny of where processors are ultimately deployed could increase.
Greater chip restrictions could weigh on sales in certain overseas markets but would not necessarily alter underlying AI demand, with compute capacity still in short supply.

AI is increasingly a geopolitical issue. Governments are watching where chips are produced, sold and deployed, which could bring tracking requirements, regulatory scrutiny and friction in supply chains, raising costs and restricting access to some overseas markets. It may also spur investment in alternative supply chains and domestic AI capacity.

UBS retains conviction in the structural AI opportunity but sees a case for more selectivity and diversification. It favors financially strong hyperscalers: tighter future compute capacity could raise the value of existing infrastructure, and lower future capex could support free cash flow.

Within AI picks and shovels (semiconductors and hardware), UBS would stay selective and favor quality companies with less margin expansion to unwind, plus defensive tech exposures such as payment networks and potential beneficiaries of lower memory costs within consumer electronics.
For investors with overly concentrated tech exposure, UBS would consider broadening within technology and diversifying across sectors, asset classes and geographies.
